newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican Zulus, National Party to talk cooperation.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican Zulus, National Party to talk cooperation.

text.p: South Africa's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party and the former ruling National Party will hold talks next week to explore a closer relationship, Inkatha chairman Ben Ngubane said on Wednesday.
After recent talks between Inkatha leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi and National Party head F.W. de Klerk, a decision was taken for senior party figures to hold further talks, Ngubane said.

KwaZulu-Natal provincial National Party leader Danie Schutte told Reuters, "It is our vision that we must bring about a balance in the political sphere and make sure South Africa does not become a one-party state," he said.
De Klerk last week disbanded a task team that was charged with forming a broad, moderate political movement to challenge President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress.
The aim of the transformation would have been to attract black voters to the party, which was seen as predominantly white and has its stronghold in the Western Cape.

Political analysts saw the disbanding of the task team as an indication of the divisions in the party over its future role and identity since it lost power to the ANC in the country's first all-race elections in 1994.

The National Party, which ruled South Africa for over 40 years and was responsible for designing and enforcing racial segregation under a policy known as apartheid, gave covert military assistance to Inkatha in the mid-1980s to counter the then-banned ANC.
About 15,000 people in the province have been killed in the brutal war between the two sides.

The Inkatha Freedom Party, which rules KwaZulu-Natal province -- home to nine million Zulus -- is a junior partner in Mandela's government, but remains one of the ANC's fiercest critics and opponents.
An Inkatha source cautioned, however, against reading too much into the talks.
"It appears the National Party is busy imploding and it doesn't come as any surprise that it is fumbling towards some sort of political configuration."
